paragraphs: Before I close forever the subject that has held me so long, I would gladly take a last look over all the different features of modern society and finally weigh the general influence that the principle of equality will have on the fate of mankind. But the difficulty of the task stops me. Faced with so great an object, my sight is clouded and my reason fails. The society of the modern world, which I have tried to describe and now try to judge, has only just come into existence. Time has not yet given it its final shape. The great revolution that created it is not yet over, and amid the events of our day it is almost impossible to tell what will pass away with the revolution itself and what will outlast it. The world that is rising is still half burdened with the remains of the world that is sinking into decay. Amid the vast confusion of human affairs, no one can say how much of the old institutions and former customs will survive, or how much will disappear entirely. The revolution now under way in the social condition, the laws, the opinions, and the feelings of men is still very far from over. Even so, its results already cannot be compared with anything the world has seen before. I go back age by age to the most distant antiquity and find nothing like what is happening before my eyes. Since the past no longer lights the way into the future, the human mind wanders in the dark. Still, in the midst of a prospect so wide, so new, and so confused, some of the more prominent features can already be made out and pointed to. The good things and the evils of life are more evenly spread across the world. Great wealth tends to vanish and small fortunes to multiply. Desires and satisfactions increase, but extraordinary prosperity and hopeless poverty are equally unknown. The feeling of ambition is universal, but its scope is seldom large. Each individual stands apart in lonely weakness, while society as a whole is active, farsighted, and powerful. What private persons accomplish is insignificant; what the state accomplishes is immense. There is little energy of character, but customs are mild and laws are humane. There are few examples of lofty heroism or of the highest, brightest, and purest virtues, but men’s habits are orderly, violence is rare, and cruelty is almost unknown. Human life grows longer and property more secure. Life is not adorned with brilliant trophies, but it is very easy and peaceful. Few pleasures are either very refined or very coarse, and highly polished manners are as uncommon as great brutality of taste. One finds neither men of great learning nor communities of extreme ignorance. Genius grows rarer and information more widespread. The human mind is moved forward by the small efforts of all mankind combined, not by the strenuous activity of certain men. There is less perfection but more abundance in everything the arts produce. The ties of race, rank, and country are loosened, and the great bond of humanity is strengthened. If I try to find the most general and most prominent of all these features, I will see that what is happening to men’s fortunes appears in a thousand other forms. Almost all extremes are softened or blunted. Everything that stood out most is replaced by some middle term, at once less lofty and less low, less brilliant and less obscure, than what the world had known before.

When I look over this countless multitude of beings, formed in one another’s likeness, among whom nothing rises and nothing falls, the sight of such universal uniformity saddens and chills me, and I am tempted to regret the state of society that has ceased to exist. When the world was full of men of great importance and extreme insignificance, of great wealth and extreme poverty, of great learning and extreme ignorance, I turned away from the latter and fixed my attention on the former alone, who pleased my sympathies. But I admit that this pleasure came from my own weakness. Because I cannot see everything around me at once, I am able to pick out and set apart the objects of my preference from among so many others. It is not so with that almighty and eternal Being whose gaze necessarily takes in all created things, and who sees mankind and man distinctly, though at the same moment. We may naturally believe that what most pleases the Creator and Preserver of men is not the singular prosperity of the few but the greater well-being of all. What seems to me a decline in man is, in His eyes, an advance; what grieves me is acceptable to Him. A state of equality is perhaps less lofty, but it is more just, and its justice makes up its greatness and its beauty. I would try, then, to raise myself to this standpoint of divine contemplation, and from there to view and judge the concerns of men.

No one on earth can yet say, absolutely and in general, that the new state of the world is better than the old one. But it is already easy to see that it is different. Some vices and some virtues were so bound up with the constitution of an aristocratic nation, and are so contrary to the character of a modern people, that they can never be instilled into it. Some good tendencies and some bad inclinations that the former never knew are natural to the latter. Some ideas come spontaneously to the imagination of one that are wholly repugnant to the mind of the other. They are like two distinct orders of human beings, each with its own merits and defects, its own advantages and its own evils. So we must take care not to judge the state of society now coming into existence by ideas drawn from a state of society that no longer exists. These two states are so different in structure that they cannot be compared justly or fairly. It would hardly be more reasonable to demand of our contemporaries the particular virtues that arose from the social condition of their forefathers, since that social condition has itself fallen and has dragged down, in one indiscriminate ruin, the good and the evil that belonged to it.

But so far these things are only imperfectly understood. I find that a great number of my contemporaries set out to make a selection from among the institutions, opinions, and ideas that arose from the aristocratic constitution of society as it was. They would gladly give up some of these elements, but they would keep the rest and transplant them into their new world. I fear that such men are wasting their time and strength in efforts that are virtuous but unprofitable. The goal is not to keep the particular advantages that inequality of conditions gave to mankind, but to secure the new benefits that equality can offer. We should not try to make ourselves like our ancestors, but strive to work out the kind of greatness and happiness that is our own. As for me, I now look back from the far end of my task and see from a distance, but all at once, the various objects that drew my closer attention along the way. I am full of fears and of hopes. I see great dangers that can be warded off, and great evils that can be avoided or lessened. And I hold more firmly to the belief that democratic nations need only will it in order to be virtuous and prosperous. I know that many of my contemporaries maintain that nations are never their own masters here below, and that they necessarily obey some unyielding and unthinking power that arises from earlier events, from their race, or from the soil and climate of their country. Such doctrines are false and cowardly, and they can never produce anything but feeble men and timid nations. Providence has not made mankind wholly independent or wholly free. It is true that a fatal circle is drawn around every man, which he cannot cross. But within the wide bounds of that circle he is powerful and free, and what is true of man is true of communities. The nations of our time cannot prevent conditions from becoming equal. But it depends on themselves whether the principle of equality leads them to servitude or to freedom, to knowledge or to barbarism, to prosperity or to wretchedness.
